sections.h2: Does Mississippi have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?
sections.html:
No. The Mississippi Department of Revenue states that Mississippi does not have an inheritance tax nor a gift tax, and that no state estate tax return is required for anyone who died on or after January 1, 2005.

Before 2005 the state collected an estate tax built on a federal credit for state death taxes. For deaths after 2004 that credit became a deduction on the federal return, so the state tax effectively went away. The old estate tax laws still sit in Title 27, Chapter 9 of the Mississippi Code, and the Uniform Estate Tax Apportionment Act is in Title 27, Chapter 10.

For an heir who wants to sell a Mississippi house, that means nobody will send you a state bill just because the house passed to you. The costs that do show up are federal rules for very large estates, income tax on any gain after the sale, property tax on the land, and the ordinary expense of recording the paperwork.

sections.h2: Where could the federal estate tax apply to a Mississippi home?
sections.html:
The federal estate tax only reaches estates above a high exclusion amount. The IRS lists a filing threshold of $15,000,000 for a 2026 year of death, and the Form 706 instructions give the same basic exclusion amount along with a basic credit amount of $5,945,800.

The same instructions put the annual gift exclusion at $19,000 per recipient for 2025 through 2026. Those numbers belong to the person who died, not to the heir, and the executor is the one who files if a return is needed.

A typical family house in Mississippi is far below that line. The Census Bureau reports a median value of owner-occupied housing units of $169,800 for 2020 to 2024. A house would only matter for the federal tax if the whole estate, counting every account and asset, passed the threshold.

sections.h2: What does an heir owe in income tax when selling an inherited house?
sections.html:
An heir owes income tax only on the gain, and the starting point is the basis. The IRS explains that the basis of property inherited from a decedent is generally its fair market value on the date of death, whether or not the executor files an estate tax return.

If the sale price is above that basis, the difference is a taxable gain. If you report a sale, it goes on Schedule D and Form 8949 of the federal return. The IRS also notes that an executor who files Form 706 may give heirs a Schedule A to Form 8971, and in that case your basis may have to match the value finally used for estate tax purposes.

This is why a date-of-death value matters even when no estate tax is due. Heirs who plan to sell often get a written appraisal for that date, because it fixes the number the gain is measured against. Ask the executor or a tax professional which value applies to your situation.

  • Keep the date-of-death appraisal or valuation letter with the sale file.
  • Keep closing statements, since selling costs reduce the gain.
  • Ask the executor whether a Schedule A to Form 8971 was issued.

sections.h2: How do property taxes work on an inherited Mississippi house?
sections.html:
Property tax follows the house, not the estate. The Department of Revenue says property is assessed each year to the owner of record on January 1, the bill is issued in November or December, and the tax is due by the following February 1.

If a parent dies in the fall and the house sits in the estate, the tax for that year still has to be paid by the date it comes due. Taxes paid to the county Tax Collector are calculated as true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate. A single-family, owner-occupied house is Class I at 10 percent of true value. An inherited house that nobody lives in is no longer owner-occupied, so it would fall into the 15 percent class for all other real property.

Unpaid taxes carry real consequences. The state FAQ says property with delinquent taxes can be sold at the county tax auction, and Mississippi gives the owner two years after the sale to redeem the property under Section 27-45-3. A house that has sat unpaid for several years is worth checking before you list it.

sections.h2: What happens to the homestead exemption when the owner dies?
sections.html:
The exemption does not pass to the heirs on its own. The Department of Revenue says a homestead exemption stays in place from year to year unless something changes, and death, deed changes, and changes in occupancy are listed as events that can require a new application.

For a buyer or heir, the filing window is January 1 through April 1 at the county Tax Assessor, and the applicant must own and occupy the home as a primary residence on January 1. Our Mississippi homestead exemption guide covers the tiers. If you sell, the new owner has to apply on their own.

sections.h2: Who handles the estate and the deed before a sale?
sections.html:
In Mississippi the county chancery clerk handles both the estate file and the land records. A county chancery clerk office describes its Chancery Court role as covering estates, guardianships, conservatorships, divorces and other equity matters, and its Recording Department records deeds, deeds of trust, releases, liens, and lis pendens.

The Department of Revenue describes the chancery clerk as the custodian of public land records, and those records are what the assessor uses to learn who owns a parcel. A new deed to the heirs or to a buyer needs to be recorded so the tax rolls match the real owner.

Recording fees are set by statute. One county clerk's schedule, effective January 1, 2020 under Section 25-7-9, lists deeds at $26.00 in an archive-fee county or $25.00 in a non-archive county for the first five pages, plus $1.00 for each extra page. Confirm the current amount with the county clerk where the house sits.

sections.h2: What should heirs check before selling a Mississippi house?
sections.html:
Start with the title, then the tax bill, then the buyer. Mississippi has no state estate tax to clear first, so the practical hurdles are paperwork and any liens.

  • Confirm who has legal authority to sign. This usually runs through the chancery court estate file.
  • Pull the county tax record and ask the Tax Collector whether anything is delinquent.
  • Check whether the house was in a tax sale and whether the two-year redemption window is still open.
  • Get a date-of-death value for the basis.
  • Ask the clerk what a deed will cost to record.
  • Ask the closing agent how this year's property tax will be divided between seller and buyer.

A cash buyer can purchase an inherited house as-is, which matters when the home needs repairs the family does not want to fund. That does not remove any of the steps above, and a buyer should not promise a price before the title and liens are known.

faqs.q: Is there an inheritance tax in Mississippi?
faqs.a: No. The Mississippi Department of Revenue says the state has no inheritance tax and no gift tax, and no state estate tax return is required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005.

faqs.q: When does the federal estate tax apply to a Mississippi estate?
faqs.a: Only when the estate is large. The IRS lists a $15,000,000 filing threshold for a 2026 year of death. Most single-family homes in the state are valued far below that, though the threshold counts the entire estate.

faqs.q: Do I pay tax when I sell a house I inherited in Mississippi?
faqs.a: You may owe federal income tax on any gain. The IRS says inherited property generally takes a basis equal to its fair market value on the date of death, so the gain is the sale price above that figure.

faqs.q: Who pays the property tax on a house in an estate?
faqs.a: Whoever holds the house when the bill is due. Mississippi assesses the owner of record on January 1, and taxes are due by February 1 of the next year. The estate or the heirs should confirm the balance with the county Tax Collector.

faqs.q: Does the homestead exemption transfer to my heirs?
faqs.a: Not automatically. The Department of Revenue lists death and deed changes among the events that can require a new application, and the filing window is January 1 to April 1 each year.
